Homonyms are two or more words that have the same spelling, or the same pronunciation, or both, but have different meanings. It is an umbrella term that includes other types of words like homophones and heteronyms.
Homophones are two or more words that have the same pronunciation but have different meanings and they may or may not be spelled the same way.
Heteronyms have the same spelling but different pronunciation.

present /prɛzənt/ - When it has the stress on the first syllable, it means something presented. In the other context, it means "a gift".
Example: I was present at the concert.
She gave me a present.

(to) present /prɪˈzɛnt/: As a verb, it means to formally talk about something.
Example: I need to present my dissertation tomorrow.

You use reported speech (indirect speech) when you are saying (reporting) what other people said or asked.

When you want to report questions, you usually use the following verbs:
ask - want to know - inquire.

How to report yes/no questions
When you report yes/no questions, you use "if" or "whether".
Example:
Direct Question
Richard: "Do you have a car?"
Reported Question
He asked me if I had a car.

How to report questions with a question word such as what, where, etc.
Direct Question
Camila: "What time does the class start?"
Tomas: "Why are you crying?"
Reported Question
She asked me what time the class started.
He wanted to know why I was crying.

Remember to change the tense of the verbs to reflect what it is going to be reported.

images.text:
Giving Effective Feedback
  • When giving feedback, acknowledge and focus on a person's behavior rather than on their personality. Address the specific behavior clearly, and then, explain your feelings about it. End with a comment stating what you expect from them after this. This model helps pinpoint behavior instead of making assumptions. For example, say, “I haven't seen you at our board meetings lately. I'm worried that you are missing important information. Can we meet soon to discuss it?” rather than, “You obviously don't think our board meetings are important!”

• Balance the content. Use the “sandwich approach”. First, you should focus on specific strengths, giving reinforcement to positive behavior and identifying exactly what the recipient ought to do. Then, point out particular things that need to be worked on and improved while you also offer solutions for change. You should always conclude with a positive point. For example: “Your speech was great. You made good eye contact and were well prepared. You were a little hard to hear at the back of the room, but with some practice you can overcome this. Keep up the good work!”, instead of, “You didn't speak loudly enough, but otherwise the speech went well.”

• Be specific. Don't make general comments as they are often of very limited use to the receiver. Give examples and alternatives that the receiver can use, but let them figure out how to use your feedback. This is better than just giving advice.
  • Be realistic. Don't waste time giving feedback on things that cannot be controlled or changed. Recipients feel empowered when they believe they have some control and can find their own solutions.
